trial_name: VSE-2 — Vasopressin, Steroids, and Epinephrine in In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (2013)
citation: Mentzelopoulos SD, Malachias S, Chamos C, Konstantopoulos D, Ntaidou T, Papastylianou A, et al. Vasopressin, Steroids, and Epinephrine and Neurologically Favorable Survival After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2013;310(3):270-279.
trial_type: RCT — multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group
one_liner: A combined vasopressin-steroids-epinephrine bundle during CPR and post-ROSC hydrocortisone improved ROSC and survival to discharge with favorable neurological outcome in vasopressor-requiring IHCA.

pico.population: Adults (>=18 years) with vasopressor-requiring in-hospital cardiac arrest.
pico.intervention: Vasopressin (20 IU/cycle) + epinephrine (1 mg/cycle) for 5 CPR cycles, methylprednisolone (40 mg IV x1) during CPR, plus hydrocortisone (300 mg/day IV for up to 7 days) for postresuscitation shock.
pico.comparison: Epinephrine (1 mg/cycle) + saline placebos during CPR and post-ROSC shock saline placebo infusion.
pico.outcome: Co-primary: ROSC >=20 minutes and survival to hospital discharge with CPC 1-2.

background.existing_knowledge: Survival with good neurological function after in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) remains poor. Epinephrine improves CPR hemodynamics and ROSC but has contested long-term effects, while vasopressin and corticosteroids may synergistically augment perfusion and attenuate post-arrest systemic inflammation.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether combining vasopressin, methylprednisolone, and epinephrine during CPR with post-ROSC hydrocortisone improves patient-centered neurological survival.
background.hypothesis: In adults with vasopressor-requiring IHCA, VSE during CPR plus stress-dose hydrocortisone for postresuscitation shock improves ROSC and survival to discharge with CPC 1-2 versus epinephrine-based standard care.

methods.design: Multicentre (3-hospital), randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial in Greece.
methods.setting: 3 hospitals (ICU/CCU, ED, wards, operating theatre); enrolled 2008-2010.

inclusion: Adults (>=18 years) with IHCA requiring vasopressor administration during CPR.
exclusion: Terminal illness with life expectancy <6 weeks or DNR order
ROSC achieved before study-drug administration (16 per group excluded post-randomisation)

methods.intervention: First 5 CPR cycles (~3 min/cycle): vasopressin 20 IU/cycle + epinephrine 1 mg/cycle; first CPR cycle: methylprednisolone 40 mg IV once. Postresuscitation shock (>4h): hydrocortisone 300 mg/day continuous IV for up to 7 days, then tapered (200 mg day 8, 100 mg day 9, then stop); hydrocortisone capped at <=3 days if acute MI present.
methods.comparison: First 5 CPR cycles: epinephrine 1 mg/cycle + saline placebo; first CPR cycle: saline placebo. Postresuscitation shock: saline placebo infusion (open-label hydrocortisone permitted clinically, cancelling study infusion).
methods.blinding: Double-blind for intra-arrest and post-arrest study infusions; syringes prepared by dedicated unblinded pharmacist.
methods.sample_size_power: Assumed CPC 1-2 survival of 4% control vs 15% VSE; alpha 0.05; power 80%; 244 patients required (300 planned to account for exclusions). Modified ITT analysis.
methods.primary_outcome: Co-primary: ROSC >=20 minutes and survival to hospital discharge with CPC 1-2.
secondary_outcomes: Poor outcome during follow-up to day 60 (death or CPC 3-5)
Epinephrine dose during advanced life support
Mean arterial pressure during CPR and ~20 min after ROSC
methods.follow_up: Daily assessment through days 1-10; clinical outcomes to day 60; CPC at hospital discharge; post hoc 1-year follow-up.

headline_bullets: VSE significantly increased ROSC >=20 minutes (83.9% vs 65.9%, OR 2.98).
VSE significantly improved survival to discharge with favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2: 13.9% vs 5.1%, OR 3.28).
The treatment effect was most pronounced in patients with postresuscitation shock (CPC 1-2: 21.1% vs 8.2%, OR 3.74).
VSE produced higher intra-arrest and post-ROSC blood pressure with lower total epinephrine requirement.

outcomes_table.outcome: Poor outcome during follow-up to day 60 (death or CPC 3-5)
Epinephrine dose during advanced life support
Mean arterial pressure during CPR (arterial line subgroup)
Mean arterial pressure ~20 min after ROSC (arterial line subgroup)

outcomes_table.note: Higher insulin exposure in steroid arm

subgroup_table.subgroup: Postresuscitation shock: CPC 1-2 survival to discharge
Postresuscitation shock: poor outcome to day 60

safety: Patient-days requiring insulin were significantly higher in the VSE group (50.4% vs 36.0%, p<0.001; target glucose <=180 mg/dL), reflecting steroid-induced hyperglycemia.

domains.notes: Computer-generated sequence (Research Randomizer v4) with pharmacy-prepared identical syringes; allocation concealed from bedside clinicians and investigators.
Double-blind setup for intra-arrest and post-arrest study drugs; CPR drug delivery was managed separately from core code team.
Modified ITT analysis; 32 of 300 randomised patients (16 per arm) were excluded after achieving ROSC prior to study drug delivery.
Post-arrest steroid separation was imperfect: 58/76 VSE shock survivors received study hydrocortisone, while 15/73 control shock survivors received open-label hydrocortisone.
Well-balanced baseline features (mean age 65.5 vs 68.2); high prevalence of non-shockable rhythms (asystole most common). Inter-center statistical heterogeneity was low (ROSC I2=0.16; CPC 1-2 I2=0).

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate due to robust double-blinding offset by post-randomisation exclusions, post-arrest steroid crossovers, and small absolute numbers of favorable neurological survivors.

domains.notes: Enrolled high-severity IHCA requiring vasopressors across typical hospital units (ICU, CCU, ED, wards, OR); excluded arrests rapidly reversed without vasopressors.
Requires rapid availability of vasopressin and steroids during resuscitation, as well as protocolised post-ROSC shock care pathways under older CPR algorithm context.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is limited-to-moderate, applying primarily to adult high-severity vasopressor-requiring IHCA with postresuscitation shock.

strengths: Patient-centred primary outcome of favorable discharge neurological survival (CPC 1-2)
Strong physiological separation demonstrated in blood pressure and organ failure-free days
Pre-specified subgroup evaluation in postresuscitation shock patients
limitations: Multicomponent bundle prevents isolating individual effect of vasopressin vs corticosteroids
Modified ITT set excluded 32 patients with early ROSC before drug delivery
Post-arrest hydrocortisone protocol deviations and open-label crossover in control arm
Small absolute number of favorable neurological survivors (18 vs 7)
Conducted across 3 Greek hospitals under older resuscitation algorithm guidelines

critical_appraisal.summary: VSE-2 demonstrates that an arrest-to-ICU drug bundle increases ROSC and discharge CPC 1-2 survival in vasopressor-requiring IHCA, though confidence is constrained by modified ITT exclusions, crossover, and small event totals.
strengths: Rigorous double-blind design with identical pharmacy-prepared syringes
Primary focus on patient-centered functional outcome (CPC 1-2)
Biologically plausible hemodynamic separation during CPR and post-ROSC
weaknesses: Open-label corticosteroid contamination in post-ROSC control arm
Small absolute difference in neurologically intact survivors (18 vs 7)

sections.authors_conclusion: Vasopressin-steroids-epinephrine during CPR and stress-dose hydrocortisone during postresuscitation shock improved ROSC and survival to discharge with CPC 1-2 in vasopressor-requiring IHCA.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Consider implementing the VSE bundle for vasopressor-requiring IHCA, particularly in patients who develop postresuscitation shock.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult patients with vasopressor-requiring in-hospital cardiac arrest and post-ROSC vasoplegic shock.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not replace rapid defibrillation, apply to promptly reversed shockable IHCA, or prove efficacy of any single bundle drug in isolation.
implementation_caveats: Requires immediate availability of vasopressin and methylprednisolone in code carts
Requires protocolised post-ROSC hydrocortisone administration (300 mg/day continuous) and taper
Requires close blood glucose monitoring due to increased insulin requirements from corticosteroid administration

controversies.notes: Multicomponent intervention combining vasopressin, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone, and lower epinephrine exposure prevents isolating the effective component.
The subsequent larger VAM-IHCA trial confirmed higher ROSC with vasopressin and methylprednisolone but failed to show statistically significant improvements in longer-term CPC 1-2 survival.
Exclusion of 32 patients achieving ROSC prior to drug administration creates potential selection bias.

context_related_trials.relation: Larger multicentre RCT testing intra-arrest vasopressin plus methylprednisolone (without post-ROSC hydrocortisone); replicated ROSC improvement but failed to confirm significant long-term functional survival benefit.

unresolved_questions: Is the neurological survival benefit dependent on the post-ROSC hydrocortisone phase?
Does VSE improve long-term survival beyond hospital discharge (1-year functional survival was not statistically significant)?
How does VSE perform within contemporary CPR algorithms and updated targeted temperature management protocols?

numbers_to_remember: MAP during CPR: 75.6 vs 52.2 mm Hg (P<0.001)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: VSE improves ROSC and discharge neurological survival in vasopressor-requiring IHCA with post-arrest shock, but wider adoption is tempered by unconfirmed long-term durability in subsequent trials.
